nodes.name: FLEECE vowel
nodes.tongue: Raise the front of your tongue high and close to the hard palate, without touching it. The tip rests behind the lower front teeth.
nodes.lips: Spread slightly, as in a relaxed smile.
nodes.jaw: Almost closed. Your teeth are only a little apart.
nodes.voicing: Voiced. Your vocal folds vibrate throughout.
nodes.airflow: Air flows smoothly over the middle of the tongue and out through the mouth.
nodes.feel: Tension along the sides of the tongue, which touch the upper side teeth. Many speakers glide slightly upward, almost like [ɪi].
nodes.note: Traditional courses call this a long vowel, but in General American the difference between /i/ and /ɪ/ is mainly tongue position and muscle tension, not length. Both get longer before a voiced consonant: seed is longer than seat.
nodes.contrast: /i/ is higher and tenser than /ɪ/, with spread lips. /ɪ/ is a relaxed, slightly lower and more central vowel.

sentences.text: We need to meet the team at three.
sentences.ipa: /wi nid tə mit ðə tim‿ət θri/

sentences.text: Please keep the key near the seat.
sentences.ipa: /pliz kip ðə ki nɪr ðə sit/

sentences.text: She sees the sea from the beach.
sentences.ipa: /ʃi siz ðə si frəm ðə bitʃ/

sentences.text: Steve eats cheese and peas.
These people believe the speech was weak.
sentences.ipa: /ðiz ˈpipl̩ bɪˈliv ðə spitʃ wəz wik/

sentences.text: Each week we read in the evening.

nodes.name: KIT vowel
nodes.tongue: Keep the front of the tongue high, but a little lower and further back than for /i/. Let it relax.
nodes.lips: Neutral and relaxed, neither spread nor rounded.
nodes.airflow: Air flows freely through the mouth.
nodes.feel: The tongue feels loose rather than tense. There is no glide; the vowel stays steady.
nodes.note: /ɪ/ is a lax vowel. It never ends a stressed word in General American, so words like see or he always use /i/, never /ɪ/.
nodes.contrast: /ɪ/ is relaxed and short-sounding. /i/ is higher and tense. /ɛ/ is lower, with the jaw more open.

sentences.text: This big fish is still in the river.
Bill will sit in the living room.
Six kids live in this little building.
Jim drinks milk with his dinner.
It is a pity the gym is busy.
Women in the city wish for quick trips.
sentences.ipa: /ˈwɪmən‿ɪn ðə ˈsɪɾi wɪʃ fɚ kwɪk trɪps/

nodes.name: DRESS vowel
nodes.tongue: The front of the tongue sits in the middle of the mouth, lower than for /ɪ/. The tip touches the back of the lower front teeth.
nodes.jaw: Half open. Drop your jaw a little more than for /ɪ/.
nodes.airflow: Air flows freely through the mouth.
nodes.feel: A relaxed, steady vowel. It should not glide toward /eɪ/.
nodes.note: Speakers of many languages make this vowel too high, close to the vowel in day. Keep the jaw open and avoid any glide.
nodes.contrast: /ɛ/ is half open. /æ/ needs a much lower jaw and tongue. /ɪ/ is higher and closer.

sentences.text: Ten friends said hello again.
Ted fed the hens bread and eggs.
The red pen is next to the bed.
sentences.ipa: /ðə rɛd pɛn‿ɪz nɛkst tə ðə bɛd/

sentences.text: Many guests left the restaurant early.
Get some rest before the test.
Ed went west to sell his best desk.
sentences.ipa: /ɛd wɛnt wɛst tə sɛl hɪz bɛst dɛsk/

nodes.name: TRAP vowel
nodes.tongue: Push the tongue low and forward. The tip presses lightly against the lower front teeth, and the body of the tongue is flat.
nodes.lips: Spread a little, as if starting a smile.
nodes.jaw: Open wide. This is one of the most open vowels in English.
nodes.airflow: Air flows freely over a low, flat tongue.
nodes.feel: You can feel the jaw drop and the tongue stretch forward. The sound is bright and somewhat long.
nodes.note: This vowel does not exist in most other languages, so learners often replace it with /ɛ/ or /ɑ/. In General American, /æ/ is often raised and gliding before m and n, so man can sound close to [mɛən]. That is a normal variant.
nodes.contrast: /æ/ is low and front with an open jaw. /ɛ/ is higher. /ʌ/ is central and relaxed. /ɑ/ is low but further back.

sentences.text: The cat sat on the black mat.
Jack has a fantastic camera.
My family traveled across Canada.
Sam ran back to grab his jacket.
sentences.ipa: /sæm ræn bæk tə ɡræb hɪz ˈdʒækət/

sentences.text: Pack an apple and a sandwich for the class.
Actually, that plan is rather bad.

nodes.name: STRUT vowel
nodes.tongue: Let the tongue rest in the center of the mouth, slightly low and slightly back. Do not push it forward or pull it far back.
nodes.airflow: Air flows freely through the mouth.
nodes.feel: This is a short, relaxed sound, close to the sound of a surprised grunt. Nothing feels tense.
nodes.note: /ʌ/ appears in stressed syllables. Its unstressed counterpart is schwa /ə/. Many learners confuse it with /ɑ/ or /æ/.
nodes.contrast: /ʌ/ is central and relaxed. /ɑ/ is lower and further back with a more open jaw. /æ/ is front and wide.

sentences.text: My brother loves running in the sun.
Come up for lunch on Monday.
Just a cup of coffee is enough.
The bus was fun until it got stuck.
Some young people come from another country.
Mother cut the onions for supper.

nodes.name: LOT / PALM vowel
nodes.tongue: Lower the tongue and pull it slightly back. The tip stays behind the lower teeth.
nodes.lips: Relaxed and unrounded. Do not round them as in British hot.
nodes.jaw: Wide open, as when a doctor asks you to say ah.
nodes.airflow: Air flows through a large, open space in the mouth.
nodes.feel: The back of your mouth feels open and spacious.
nodes.note: In General American, words like hot, stop, and box use this unrounded /ɑ/, the same vowel as in father. Many Americans also use it in caught and thought, a pattern called the cot and caught merger.
nodes.contrast: /ɑ/ is low and back with an open jaw and no rounding. /ʌ/ is higher and central. /oʊ/ starts rounded and glides.

sentences.text: Bob got a hot coffee at the shop.
sentences.ipa: /bɑb ɡɑɾ‿ə hɑt ˈkɑfi ət ðə ʃɑp/

sentences.text: Stop the clock at the top of the hour.
sentences.ipa: /stɑp ðə klɑk‿ət ðə tɑp‿əv ði ˈaʊɚ/

sentences.text: My father has a lot of odd jobs.
Tom dropped the box on the rocks.
The doctor wants a calm, honest answer.
Watch the dog on the dock.

nodes.name: Schwa
nodes.tongue: Let the whole tongue rest in the middle of the mouth, completely relaxed.
nodes.lips: Neutral. Do not spread or round them.
nodes.jaw: Slightly open, just enough to let sound out.
nodes.airflow: A short, weak burst of air through a relaxed mouth.
nodes.feel: Very quick and effortless. It sounds like a short, neutral uh.
nodes.note: Schwa is the most common vowel in English, and it appears only in unstressed syllables. It can be spelled with any vowel letter. Reducing unstressed vowels to schwa is essential for natural American rhythm.
nodes.contrast: Listen for the tiny, quick vowel before the stressed syllable. Without schwa, support becomes sport and parade becomes prayed.

sentences.text: A banana is a good snack today.
The police arrived at about seven.
Ask the woman about the problem.
Canada is a pleasant place to visit.
The lemon is on the sofa.
Support the local family business.

nodes.name: GOOSE vowel
nodes.tongue: Raise the back of the tongue high toward the soft palate. In American English it is often a little more central than in other accents.
nodes.lips: Rounded and pushed slightly forward, as if blowing out a candle.
nodes.airflow: Air flows through the small, rounded opening of the lips.
nodes.feel: Firm lip rounding and tension in the tongue. Many speakers glide slightly, like [ʊu].
nodes.note: After t, d, n, and s, General American usually drops the /j/ sound: new is /nu/ and student is /ˈstudənt/, unlike British /nju/.
nodes.contrast: /u/ is high, tense, and strongly rounded. /ʊ/ is lower, shorter-sounding, and only lightly rounded.

sentences.text: Sue moved to a new school in June.
sentences.ipa: /su muvd tu ə nu skul‿ɪn dʒun/

sentences.text: The food in the room was cool.
Who knew the truth about the blue shoes?
sentences.ipa: /hu nu ðə truθ‿əˈbaʊt ðə blu ʃuz/

sentences.text: Lucy chose soup and fruit.
Do you have two spoons?
The group flew to Peru.

nodes.name: FOOT vowel
nodes.tongue: Keep the back of the tongue fairly high, but lower and more relaxed than for /u/.
nodes.lips: Lightly rounded, much less than for /u/.
nodes.airflow: Air flows through a relaxed, lightly rounded opening.
nodes.feel: Loose and short. If your lips feel tight, you are probably making /u/ instead.
nodes.note: /ʊ/ is a lax vowel found in a small but very common set of words such as good, could, would, and should.
nodes.contrast: /ʊ/ is relaxed and lightly rounded. /u/ is tense with firm rounding. /ʌ/ has no rounding at all.

sentences.text: Look at the good book on the shelf.
The woman put sugar in her cookies.
sentences.ipa: /ðə ˈwʊmən pʊt ˈʃʊɡɚ ɪn hɝ ˈkʊkiz/

sentences.text: Could you push the wood a bit?
He took a step with his left foot.
sentences.ipa: /hi tʊk‿ə stɛp wɪð hɪz lɛft fʊt/

sentences.text: I should have stood by the brook.
sentences.ipa: /aɪ ʃʊd hæv stʊd baɪ ðə brʊk/

sentences.text: Would you cook the pudding?

nodes.name: THOUGHT vowel
nodes.tongue: Keep the tongue low and back, slightly higher than for /ɑ/.
nodes.jaw: Open, but a little less than for /ɑ/.
nodes.airflow: Air flows through a large space at the back of the mouth.
nodes.feel: Similar to /ɑ/, with a touch of lip rounding.
nodes.note: Many Americans pronounce this vowel exactly like /ɑ/, so caught and cot sound the same. Both pronunciations are standard. The important contrast to master is /ɔ/ versus /oʊ/, as in law and low.
nodes.contrast: /ɔ/ is a steady low back vowel. /oʊ/ starts higher and glides toward a rounded /ʊ/.

sentences.text: We saw a small dog in the hall.
sentences.ipa: /wi sɔ ə smɔl dɔɡ‿ɪn ðə hɔl/

sentences.text: Paul bought a long cloth.
Talk to your daughter about the law.
sentences.ipa: /tɔk tə jɚ ˈdɔɾɚ əˈbaʊt ðə lɔ/

sentences.text: I thought the walk was awful.
The ball fell off the wall.
Dawn caught a cold in August.

nodes.name: Voiceless bilabial stop
nodes.tongue: The tongue rests in a neutral position and is free to prepare the next sound.
nodes.lips: Press both lips together firmly to block the air, then release them suddenly.
nodes.jaw: Closed for the hold, then opens for the following vowel.
nodes.voicing: Voiceless. Your vocal folds do not vibrate during the closure.
nodes.airflow: Air pressure builds behind the closed lips and escapes in a small burst.
nodes.feel: At the start of a stressed syllable, hold a hand in front of your mouth: you should feel a clear puff of air.
nodes.note: That puff is called aspiration, written [pʰ]. Without it, Americans may hear /b/. After s, as in sport, /p/ is not aspirated.
nodes.contrast: /p/ is voiceless and aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable. /b/ is voiced and has no puff of air.

sentences.text: Peter put the paper in his pocket.
sentences.ipa: /ˈpiɾɚ pʊt ðə ˈpeɪpɚ ɪn hɪz ˈpɑkɪt/

sentences.text: Please pass the pepper.
Pam picked a pink pen.
Stop the people at the top of the steps.
sentences.ipa: /stɑp ðə ˈpipl̩‿ət ðə tɑp‿əv ðə stɛps/

sentences.text: The puppy played in the park.
Paul's plan was perfect.

nodes.name: Voiced bilabial stop
nodes.tongue: Neutral, ready for the next sound.
nodes.lips: Close both lips gently, then release.
nodes.voicing: Voiced. At the start of a word, American /b/ often has only a little voicing, but it never has a puff of air.
nodes.airflow: Air is held briefly behind the lips and released without a burst of breath.
nodes.feel: A soft release with no strong puff. At the end of a word, the vowel before /b/ is noticeably longer than before /p/.
nodes.note: Final /b/ must not turn into /p/. Keep the vowel before it long: cab is longer than cap.
nodes.contrast: /b/ is made with both lips closed. /v/ uses the upper teeth on the lower lip and lets air through. /p/ is voiceless with a puff of air.

sentences.text: Bob bought a big blue bag.
The baby's bottle is on the table.
Ben grabbed the rubber ball.
Bring a bigger box to the club.
The bus broke down by the bridge.
sentences.ipa: /ðə bʌs broʊk daʊn baɪ ðə brɪdʒ/

sentences.text: Both brothers bake bread.

nodes.name: Voiceless alveolar stop
nodes.tongue: Press the tip of the tongue against the alveolar ridge, the bump just behind the upper front teeth. Not against the teeth.
nodes.airflow: Air is blocked by the tongue tip and released in a burst, aspirated at the start of stressed syllables.
nodes.feel: A crisp tap of the tongue tip on the ridge, followed by a puff of air in words like ten and time.
nodes.note: American /t/ has several forms: aspirated in ten, a quick flap in water, often unreleased at the end of a word, and sometimes a glottal stop before n, as in button.
nodes.contrast: /t/ is voiceless and aspirated. /d/ is voiced with no puff. /θ/ is a soft continuous hiss with the tongue at the teeth.

sentences.text: Tom took two tickets to Texas.
Turn the table toward the light.
Tell Tina it's time to start.
Kate wrote a short test.
Stand still at the start line.
The tall tree stood next to the tent.
sentences.ipa: /ðə tɔl tri stʊd nɛkst tə ðə tɛnt/

nodes.name: Voiced alveolar stop
nodes.tongue: The tongue tip presses on the alveolar ridge behind the upper teeth.
nodes.airflow: Air is held briefly and released without a puff.
nodes.feel: A soft tap at the ridge. The vowel before a final /d/ is longer than before /t/.
nodes.note: English /d/ is made on the ridge, not on the teeth as in many other languages. Final /d/ should not become /t/.
nodes.contrast: /d/ is a stop at the ridge. /ð/ is a continuous voiced sound with the tongue at the teeth. /t/ is voiceless.

sentences.text: Dad drove down the road.
David did the dishes after dinner.
The old dog hid under the bed.
Did you find the gold ring?
Diane loved the red dress.
Send the cards today.

nodes.name: Voiceless velar stop
nodes.tongue: Raise the back of the tongue against the soft palate to block the air.
nodes.airflow: Air builds up behind the back of the tongue and is released with a puff in stressed syllables.
nodes.feel: Contact far back in the mouth, then a clear burst of breath in key and cat.
nodes.note: Like /p/ and /t/, /k/ is aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable and unaspirated after s, as in sky.
nodes.contrast: /k/ is voiceless and aspirated. /ɡ/ is voiced and has no puff of air.

sentences.text: Kate keeps the keys in the kitchen.
Can you carry the cake carefully?
Ken cooked a quick snack.
Look at the clock on the cabinet.
The kids kicked the ball back.
Call the clerk about the ticket.

nodes.name: Voiced velar stop
nodes.tongue: The back of the tongue presses against the soft palate.
nodes.airflow: Air is held and released gently, with no puff.
nodes.feel: Contact at the back of the mouth with the throat buzzing.
nodes.note: At the end of a word, keep /ɡ/ voiced and lengthen the vowel before it: bag is longer than back.
nodes.contrast: /ɡ/ is voiced with no puff. /k/ is voiceless and aspirated.

sentences.text: Greg gave the girl a green bag.
Go get the eggs from the garden.
sentences.ipa: /ɡoʊ ɡɛt ði ɛɡz frəm ðə ˈɡɑrdn̩/

sentences.text: The big dog dug in the grass.
Grandma grew grapes again.
The guests begged for good games.
Give the glass to Gary.

nodes.name: Aspiration
nodes.tongue: Depends on the stop: lips for /p/, the ridge for /t/, the soft palate for /k/.
nodes.lips: For /p/, close the lips and release them with force.
nodes.jaw: Opens for the vowel right after the release.
nodes.voicing: Voiceless. Voicing for the vowel starts a fraction of a second after the release.
nodes.airflow: A strong puff of breath follows the release, before the vowel begins.
nodes.feel: Hold a sheet of paper in front of your lips. Say pie: the paper should move. Say spy: it should barely move.
nodes.note: Aspiration is not a separate phoneme in English. It is a variant of /p/, /t/, and /k/ that appears at the start of stressed syllables. Speakers of languages without it often sound as if they are saying /b/, /d/, or /ɡ/.
nodes.contrast: Aspirated /p t k/ carry a puff of air before the vowel. /b d ɡ/ have none, so the vowel starts immediately.

sentences.text: Pat talked to Kate at the party.
Put two cups on the table.
Can Tom keep the top part?
The car parked in a tight spot.
Ten people came at two.
Keep calm and take your time.

nodes.name: Bilabial nasal
nodes.tongue: Relaxed and resting.
nodes.lips: Close the lips gently and keep them closed.
nodes.airflow: The soft palate lowers, so all the air goes out through the nose.
nodes.feel: A hum. Touch the side of your nose and you will feel it vibrate.
nodes.note: Keep final /m/ fully closed. Opening the lips too early can make some sound like sun.
nodes.contrast: /m/ closes the lips. /n/ keeps the lips open and closes with the tongue tip on the ridge.

sentences.text: My mother makes muffins every morning.
Come home in the summer.
Mark met Mia at the museum.
Tim moved to a small farm.
Many men climb the mountain.
Mom smiled at me.

nodes.name: Alveolar nasal
nodes.tongue: Press the tongue tip on the alveolar ridge and seal the sides of the tongue against the upper teeth.
nodes.airflow: Air is blocked in the mouth and flows out through the nose.
nodes.feel: Humming through the nose with the tongue tip on the ridge.
nodes.note: At the end of a word, make sure the tongue tip actually reaches the ridge. Otherwise the vowel may simply become nasal.
nodes.contrast: /n/ is made with the tongue tip on the ridge. /ŋ/ is made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate.

sentences.text: Nancy needs nine new notebooks.
Ten men ran to the station.
Never answer the phone at night.
Nobody knew the name of the town.
Dan is in the kitchen now.
Ann opened the window.

nodes.name: Velar nasal
nodes.tongue: Raise the back of the tongue against the soft palate, as for /k/, while the tip stays down.
nodes.airflow: Air flows only through the nose.
nodes.feel: A hum at the back of the mouth. The tongue tip should not touch the ridge.
nodes.note: In General American, singer has no /ɡ/ after /ŋ/: /ˈsɪŋɚ/. But finger and longer do include /ɡ/. Do not add a /k/ or /ɡ/ at the end of sing.
nodes.contrast: /ŋ/ uses the back of the tongue. /n/ uses the tip on the ridge.

sentences.text: The singer is singing a long song.
Bring the ring to the king.
I think the young man is waiting.
Thanks for bringing the drink.
Morning running is relaxing.
Hang the painting in the hallway.

nodes.name: FACE diphthong
nodes.tongue: Start with the tongue in the /ɛ/ area and glide upward toward /ɪ/.
nodes.jaw: Starts half open and closes a little during the glide.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow while the tongue moves.
nodes.feel: You should feel movement: the vowel is not a single steady sound.
nodes.note: Without the glide, /eɪ/ can sound like /ɛ/, so late may be heard as let. The glide is longer in stressed syllables.
nodes.contrast: /eɪ/ glides upward toward /ɪ/. /ɛ/ stays still and is slightly lower.

sentences.text: They came late to the train station.
sentences.ipa: /ðeɪ keɪm leɪt tə ðə treɪn ˈsteɪʃən/

sentences.text: Take a break and stay a day.
Jane made a cake for the neighbors.
The rain in Spain stays mainly in the plain.
sentences.ipa: /ðə reɪn‿ɪn speɪn steɪz ˈmeɪnli ɪn ðə pleɪn/

sentences.text: Eight great players came to play.
Wait for the table by the gate.
sentences.ipa: /weɪt fɚ ðə ˈteɪbəl baɪ ðə ɡeɪt/

nodes.name: GOAT diphthong
nodes.tongue: Start with the tongue in the middle, slightly back, and glide up and back toward /ʊ/.
nodes.lips: Start lightly rounded and round more during the glide.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow through rounding lips.
nodes.feel: Your lips move forward and close during the vowel.
nodes.note: A pure /o/ without the glide sounds foreign in American English. Make the rounding movement clear.
nodes.contrast: /oʊ/ is rounded and glides. /ɑ/ is open, unrounded, and steady.

sentences.text: Joe drove home alone.
Don't go out in the snow.
I hope the boat floats slowly.
Show me the phone you own.
Rose wrote a note to Tony.
Most of the old roads are closed.

nodes.name: PRICE diphthong
nodes.tongue: Start low and central with an open mouth, then raise the front of the tongue toward /ɪ/.
nodes.jaw: Starts wide open and closes noticeably.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow during a large tongue movement.
nodes.feel: A big movement from open to almost closed.
nodes.note: Before voiceless consonants, many Americans start this diphthong a little higher, so the vowel in write differs slightly from ride.
nodes.contrast: /aɪ/ starts with an open jaw. /eɪ/ starts much higher, so its movement is smaller.

sentences.text: I like to ride my bike at night.
sentences.ipa: /aɪ laɪk tə raɪd maɪ baɪk‿ət naɪt/

sentences.text: Mike tried to find the right size.
sentences.ipa: /maɪk traɪd tə faɪnd ðə raɪt saɪz/

sentences.text: Five white lights shine in the sky.
Why did you hide the knife?
Try the rice and the pie.
My wife writes nice poems.

nodes.name: MOUTH diphthong
nodes.tongue: Start low and open, then raise the back of the tongue toward /ʊ/.
nodes.lips: Start unrounded and round them at the end.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow while lips round.
nodes.feel: The lips move from open to rounded, as if saying ow after touching something hot.
nodes.note: Make sure the glide ends with rounding. Without it, now can sound like no or like a flat /a/.
nodes.contrast: /aʊ/ starts open and glides to rounded lips. /oʊ/ starts higher. /ɑ/ does not move at all.

sentences.text: How about a walk around the town?
The crowd shouted loudly outside.
Count the flowers on the ground.
Our house is south of the mountain.
Now sit down on the couch.
I found a mouse in the house.

nodes.name: CHOICE diphthong
nodes.tongue: Start low and back, then move the tongue forward and up toward /ɪ/.
nodes.lips: Start rounded and spread them as you glide.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow.
nodes.feel: Lips change from rounded to spread.
nodes.note: This diphthong is relatively rare but clear. Keep the rounding at the beginning so boy does not sound like buy.
nodes.contrast: /ɔɪ/ starts with rounded lips at the back. /aɪ/ starts open and central with no rounding.

sentences.text: The boy enjoyed his new toy.
Roy made a good choice.
Avoid the noise of the boiling oil.
Joy pointed at the coin.
Her voice was full of joy.
The employer annoyed the loyal employee.

nodes.name: Voiceless labiodental fricative
nodes.tongue: Relaxed and low.
nodes.lips: Lightly touch the lower lip to the upper front teeth.
nodes.airflow: Air hisses continuously through the narrow gap between teeth and lip.
nodes.feel: Air on your lower lip and no vibration in the throat.
nodes.note: Keep the contact light. Pressing hard can stop the air and produce a /p/-like sound.
nodes.contrast: /f/ is voiceless. /v/ has the same position with voicing. /p/ stops the air completely at the lips.

sentences.text: Fill the cup with fresh coffee.
Phil laughed at the funny photo.
The fish swam off fast.
Few families feel safe here.
Fold the flag after the film.
Five friends found a fine gift.

nodes.name: Voiced labiodental fricative
nodes.tongue: Relaxed.
nodes.lips: The upper teeth rest lightly on the inside of the lower lip.
nodes.voicing: Voiced. You should feel a buzz in the throat and on the lip.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow through the teeth and lip, with voicing.
nodes.feel: Your lower lip tickles. If your lips round and do not touch the teeth, you are making /w/.
nodes.note: Speakers of many languages confuse /v/ and /w/. For /v/, the teeth must touch the lip. For /w/, the teeth do not touch anything.
nodes.contrast: /v/ needs the upper teeth on the lower lip. /w/ is made with rounded lips that do not touch the teeth. /b/ closes both lips.

sentences.text: Vicky loves visiting the village.
Victor gave Vera seven violets.
We have a very vivid view of the river.
sentences.ipa: /wi hæv‿ə ˈvɛri ˈvɪvəd vju əv ðə ˈrɪvɚ/

sentences.text: Never leave the van in the valley.
Steve drove over the river.
Five vans arrived in the evening.

nodes.name: Voiceless alveolar fricative
nodes.tongue: Bring the tongue tip close to the alveolar ridge without touching it. Form a narrow groove down the middle of the tongue.
nodes.airflow: A narrow jet of air rushes through the groove and hits the teeth.
nodes.feel: A sharp, high hiss.
nodes.note: If the tongue touches the teeth, /s/ can turn into /θ/, a lisp. Keep the tip behind the ridge.
nodes.contrast: /s/ is a sharp hiss behind the ridge. /θ/ is softer, with the tongue against the back of the upper teeth.

sentences.text: Sam sells soft socks.
Sit still and listen to the silence.
Sarah saw seven ships at sea.
Pass the salt and the rice.
The bus stops at six.
Steve speaks slowly and softly.

nodes.name: Voiced alveolar fricative
nodes.tongue: Same position as /s/: the tip close to the ridge with a central groove.
nodes.voicing: Voiced. You should feel a buzz.
nodes.airflow: A narrow jet of air with voicing.
nodes.feel: A buzzing hiss, like a bee.
nodes.note: Plural and verb endings are often /z/: dogs, plays, is. Many learners devoice them to /s/. Keep the vowel before final /z/ long: eyes is longer than ice.
nodes.contrast: /z/ is voiced and makes the vowel before it longer. /s/ is voiceless and shortens the vowel.

sentences.text: Zoe's zebra is lazy.
These roses are amazing.
Is the music too noisy?
His dogs always lose their toys.
Please close the windows.
Lisa was busy on Tuesday.

nodes.name: Voiceless postalveolar fricative
nodes.tongue: Pull the tongue slightly back from the /s/ position, behind the alveolar ridge, with a wider, flatter channel.
nodes.airflow: A broad stream of air through a wide channel.
nodes.feel: A lower, softer hush than /s/, like asking someone to be quiet.
nodes.note: Lip rounding is an important part of English /ʃ/. Without it, the sound can be heard as /s/.
nodes.contrast: /ʃ/ is further back with rounded lips. /s/ is a sharp hiss with spread lips. /tʃ/ starts with a stop.

sentences.text: She sells seashells by the seashore.
Shut the shop at night.
Sharon washed the dishes.
I wish the ocean was shallow.
Show me the machine at the station.
Make sure the fish is fresh.

nodes.name: Voiced postalveolar fricative
nodes.tongue: Same position as /ʃ/: just behind the alveolar ridge with a wide channel.
nodes.airflow: A broad stream of air with voicing.
nodes.feel: A soft buzzing hush.
nodes.note: /ʒ/ is the least frequent consonant in English. It usually appears in the middle of words such as measure and vision, and at the end of a few borrowed words such as beige and garage.
nodes.contrast: /ʒ/ is voiced and continuous. /ʃ/ is its voiceless partner. /dʒ/ begins with a stop.

sentences.text: Measure the treasure with pleasure.
It is usual to watch television at leisure.
The beige garage looks unusual.
We usually visit Asia in June.
Her decision was a pleasure to hear.
His vision of the treasure was unusual.

nodes.name: Voiceless postalveolar affricate
nodes.tongue: Press the front of the tongue just behind the alveolar ridge, then release it slowly into /ʃ/.
nodes.airflow: A short stop followed by a hush of air.
nodes.feel: A stop and a hiss blended into one sound.
nodes.note: /tʃ/ is one sound, not two. Its release is quick and aspirated at the start of stressed syllables.
nodes.contrast: /tʃ/ begins with a complete stop. /ʃ/ is continuous from the start.

sentences.text: Charlie chose cheese for lunch.
The teacher checked each chapter.
Watch the children in the kitchen.
Which chair is cheaper?
Catch the chicken by the church.
Chuck watched the match in the kitchen.

nodes.name: Voiced postalveolar affricate
nodes.tongue: Press the tongue just behind the ridge and release it into /ʒ/.
nodes.airflow: A short stop followed by a voiced hush.
nodes.feel: A buzzing version of /tʃ/.
nodes.note: At the end of words such as age and bridge, keep /dʒ/ voiced and the vowel before it long.
nodes.contrast: /dʒ/ is voiced. /tʃ/ is voiceless. /j/, as in yet, has no stop and no friction.

sentences.text: John enjoys orange juice.
George jumped over the large bridge.
Jenny's job is just a joke.
The judge changed the page.
Jack gently packed the jacket.
Jill visited Germany in June.

nodes.name: Voiceless glottal fricative
nodes.tongue: Already in position for the following vowel.
nodes.jaw: Open as for the following vowel.
nodes.airflow: A gentle breath of air from the throat, with no friction in the mouth.
nodes.feel: Like fogging a mirror with your breath.
nodes.note: English /h/ is much softer than the scraping sound at the back of the mouth found in Russian or German. Do not drop it either: hair and air are different words.
nodes.contrast: With /h/, a soft breath comes before the vowel. Without it, the vowel starts directly.

sentences.text: Harry has a huge house on the hill.
Hold her hand and help her.
How happy he looks today!
Hannah hid behind the hedge.
Have you heard the history of Hawaii?
sentences.ipa: /hæv ju hɝd ðə ˈhɪstəri əv həˈwaɪi/

sentences.text: Hurry home before the hail.

nodes.name: Voiceless dental fricative
nodes.tongue: Place the tip of the tongue lightly against the back of the upper front teeth or just between the teeth.
nodes.airflow: Air flows continuously over the tongue and between the teeth. It never stops.
nodes.feel: Cool air on the tip of your tongue. If the air stops, you are making /t/. If the tongue pulls back, you are making /s/.
nodes.note: /θ/ is rare in the world's languages, so learners often replace it with /s/, /t/, or /f/. Americans understand these substitutions, but they can change the meaning: think versus sink.
nodes.contrast: /θ/ is soft and continuous at the teeth. /s/ is sharp, behind the ridge. /t/ stops the air. /f/ uses the lip.

sentences.text: I think three is the right number.
sentences.ipa: /aɪ θɪŋk θri ɪz ðə raɪt ˈnʌmbɚ/

sentences.text: Thank you for the thoughtful birthday gift.
sentences.ipa: /θæŋk ju fɚ ðə ˈθɔtfəl ˈbɝθdeɪ ɡɪft/

sentences.text: Both of them are healthy and strong.
Ruth threw the thick cloth.
Thursday is the thirtieth of the month.
Keith thanked Beth for the theater tickets.
sentences.ipa: /kiθ θæŋkt bɛθ fɚ ðə ˈθiəɾɚ ˈtɪkəts/

nodes.name: Voiced dental fricative
nodes.tongue: Same as /θ/: the tongue tip lightly touches the back of the upper teeth.
nodes.voicing: Voiced. You should feel a buzz on the tip of your tongue.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow with voicing.
nodes.feel: A gentle buzz between tongue and teeth.
nodes.note: /ð/ appears in the most common words in English: the, this, that, they, there. In fast speech it can be very short, but it should not become a hard /d/ or /z/.
nodes.contrast: /ð/ is voiced and continuous at the teeth. /d/ stops at the ridge. /z/ is a hiss behind the ridge.

sentences.text: This is my mother and father.
They gathered together over there.
The weather is smoother than that.
My brother bathes the dog.
Neither of them breathed.
Those are the other clothes.

nodes.name: Labial-velar approximant
nodes.tongue: Raise the back of the tongue toward the soft palate, as for /u/.
nodes.lips: Round them tightly and push them forward, then quickly open into the vowel.
nodes.airflow: Air flows freely. There is no friction.
nodes.feel: A quick movement of the lips from tight rounding to the next vowel. The teeth never touch the lips.
nodes.note: /w/ behaves like a very short /u/ that glides into the following vowel.
nodes.contrast: /w/ uses rounded lips only. /v/ needs the upper teeth on the lower lip.

sentences.text: We went west on Wednesday.
William wants a glass of warm water.
Why are the windows wet?
The wind was wild all week.
Wendy walked away quietly.
One woman won twice.

nodes.name: Palatal approximant
nodes.tongue: Raise the front of the tongue high toward the hard palate, as for /i/, then glide into the vowel.
nodes.airflow: Free airflow without friction.
nodes.feel: A quick glide from an /i/ position.
nodes.note: The IPA symbol /j/ stands for the sound of English y, not the sound of English j. It also hides inside words like use and music.
nodes.contrast: /j/ is a smooth glide. /dʒ/ starts with a stop and has friction.

sentences.text: Your young cousin is a year older.
Yes, you can use the yellow cup.
sentences.ipa: /jɛs | ju kən juz ðə ˈjɛloʊ kʌp/

sentences.text: A few young musicians played beautiful music.
sentences.ipa: /ə fju jʌŋ mjuˈzɪʃənz pleɪd ˈbjuɾəfəl ˈmjuzɪk/

sentences.text: Yesterday you said yes.
The yard is used every year.
You knew the youth club was huge.
sentences.ipa: /ju nu ðə juθ klʌb wəz hjudʒ/

nodes.name: Alveolar lateral approximant
nodes.tongue: Touch the tongue tip to the alveolar ridge and let the sides of the tongue drop.
nodes.airflow: Air flows around the sides of the tongue.
nodes.feel: The tip stays on the ridge while sound escapes at the sides.
nodes.note: At the beginning of a syllable, American /l/ is relatively light. At the end of a syllable it becomes dark. See the Dark L lesson.
nodes.contrast: For /l/, the tongue tip touches the ridge. For /ɹ/, the tip touches nothing and the tongue bunches back.

sentences.text: Lily loves lemon lollipops.
Look at the lovely yellow light.
Lucy laughed a lot at lunch.
Please play the flute slowly.
The blue lake is lovely.
Larry lives alone in London.

nodes.name: Dark L
nodes.tongue: The tip may touch the ridge, but the back of the tongue also rises toward the soft palate, as for /ʊ/.
nodes.airflow: Air flows around the sides of the tongue.
nodes.feel: A deep, hollow l, close to the vowel in book. The vowel before it often glides toward it, as in feel [fiəɫ].
nodes.note: Dark L is not a separate phoneme. It is the form /l/ takes at the end of a syllable, in words like call, milk, and people. In American English, even initial /l/ is somewhat dark compared with many other languages.
nodes.contrast: Listen for the hollow /ɫ/ at the end. Without it, goal becomes go and while becomes why.

sentences.text: I feel cold in the hall.
Bill will call the school.
Fill the bottle with milk.
Paul held the small ball.
The whole world is full of people.
Help yourself to the apple pie.

nodes.name: American R
nodes.tongue: Either curl the tongue tip up and slightly back without touching anything, or bunch the body of the tongue up and back. The sides touch the upper back teeth.
nodes.lips: Slightly rounded, especially at the start of a word.
nodes.airflow: Air flows freely over the tongue. There is no tap and no trill.
nodes.feel: The tongue tip floats in the air. If it taps the ridge, you are making a different sound.
nodes.note: Dictionaries usually write this sound as /r/, but the American sound is an approximant, transcribed /ɹ/ in precise IPA. It is never rolled.
nodes.contrast: /ɹ/ has a floating tongue tip and rounded lips. /l/ touches the ridge. /w/ uses only the lips.

sentences.text: Robert reads really great stories.
The red car rolled into the river.
Rachel wrote three letters.
Rain ruined our trip to Rome.
Rick rarely runs in the rain.
Are you ready for the right answer?

nodes.name: NURSE vowel
nodes.tongue: Pull the tongue back and bunch it up in the middle, or curl the tip slightly back. The tip does not touch anything.
nodes.airflow: Air flows over a bunched tongue, which gives the vowel its r-color.
nodes.feel: The whole vowel is r-colored from start to finish. It is not a vowel followed by r.
nodes.note: /ɝ/ is stressed, as in bird. /ɚ/ is its unstressed form, as in teacher. Do not add a separate vowel before the r.
nodes.contrast: /ɝ/ is r-colored all the way through, with the tongue bunched in the middle. /ɑr/ starts with an open /ɑ/ and then adds r.

sentences.text: The girl heard the third bird.
Learn the words before Thursday.
Her brother works early.
The nurse turned the curtain.
My sister prefers the purple shirt.
Herb served dessert first.

nodes.name: START vowel
nodes.tongue: Start with a low, back /ɑ/, then lift and pull the tongue back for r.
nodes.lips: Unrounded at the start, slightly rounded at the end.
nodes.jaw: Starts wide open and closes a little.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow.
nodes.feel: A clear open vowel that bends into r.
nodes.note: General American is rhotic: the r is always pronounced after a vowel, unlike in many British accents.
nodes.contrast: /ɑr/ begins with an open /ɑ/. /ɝ/ is r-colored from the very beginning with a more closed jaw.

sentences.text: Park the car in the yard.
Mark started the party after dark.
The farmer's barn is far away.
Charles has a large garden.
Start the car and drive far.
Barbara carved the cards.

nodes.name: NORTH / FORCE vowel
nodes.tongue: Start in the /ɔ/ or /o/ area, low to mid and back, then add r.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow.
nodes.feel: Rounded lips and a vowel that bends into r.
nodes.note: In General American, north and force have merged, so for and four share this vowel.
nodes.contrast: /ɔr/ starts with rounded lips and a back vowel. /ɝ/ is r-colored from the start. /ɑr/ starts open and unrounded.

sentences.text: George ordered more orange juice.
The horse ran north in the storm.
Close the door before the morning.
Laura's story is boring.
The sports court is short.
Four doors were already open.

nodes.name: NEAR vowel
nodes.tongue: Start high and front, then pull the tongue back into r.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow.
nodes.feel: A short high vowel that slides into r.
nodes.note: Learners often insert a separate vowel, making here sound like two syllables. Keep it as one smooth syllable.
nodes.contrast: /ɪr/ starts high, close to /ɪ/. /ɛr/ starts lower, with the jaw more open.

sentences.text: We hear the deer near here.
Cheers to a great new year!
The engineer appears nearly every year.
Dear, the beer is here.
Steer clear of the pier.
Her career is clearly important.

nodes.name: SQUARE vowel
nodes.tongue: Start mid and front, as for /ɛ/, then pull the tongue back into r.
nodes.airflow: Continuous airflow.
nodes.feel: One syllable: a mid vowel that bends into r.
nodes.note: In General American, Mary, marry, and merry are usually pronounced the same, all with this vowel.
nodes.contrast: /ɛr/ starts mid and front. /ɪr/ starts higher. /ɑr/ starts low and back.

sentences.text: Where is the chair with the pear?
Take care on the stairs.
Their bear is very rare.
Mary shares her hair care tips.
The airport is over there.
Clare stared at the square.

nodes.name: Flap T
nodes.tongue: Flick the tongue tip quickly against the alveolar ridge, once, like a very fast /d/.
nodes.voicing: Voiced. The voicing of the vowels continues through the flap.
nodes.airflow: Airflow is interrupted for only a moment.
nodes.feel: A light, quick tap, much shorter than a normal /t/ or /d/.
nodes.note: The flap is an allophone of /t/ and /d/. It appears between vowels when the next syllable is unstressed, as in water, city, and ladder, and across words, as in get it. As a result, writer and rider, or latter and ladder, can sound the same.
nodes.contrast: A flap appears between vowels before an unstressed syllable. When the T starts a stressed syllable, as in attack or hotel, it stays a true, aspirated T.

sentences.text: I'd like a bottle of water, please.
It's a pretty city.
Put it on the computer.
We met at a party.
Wait a little bit.
It doesn't matter at all.

nodes.name: Final voicing contrast
nodes.tongue: Depends on the consonant. The key difference is not the consonant itself but the length of the vowel before it.
nodes.jaw: Hold the vowel slightly longer before a voiced consonant.
nodes.voicing: Final voiced consonants are only partly voiced in English. Listeners rely mainly on vowel length.
nodes.airflow: Before a voiceless consonant, the vowel is clipped short and the airflow stops abruptly.
nodes.feel: Bed sounds long and smooth. Bet sounds short and clipped.
nodes.note: In Russian, German, and many other languages, final voiced consonants become voiceless. English keeps the contrast, and the vowel length carries most of it. Lengthening the vowel is the most effective way to be understood.
nodes.contrast: Before a voiced consonant, the vowel is long. Before a voiceless consonant, it is short and clipped.

sentences.text: Put the bag in the back.
The dog dug a hole in the sand.
Save the prize for later.
His eyes are as cold as ice.
Read the card at the side door.
Leave the cab by the gate.

nodes.name: Syllabic consonants
nodes.tongue: Keep the tongue tip on the alveolar ridge from the /t/ or /d/ straight into /n/ or /l/, with no vowel in between.
nodes.voicing: Voiced. The /n/ or /l/ itself forms the syllable.
nodes.airflow: For button, the air is released through the nose. For little, it is released over the sides of the tongue.
nodes.feel: The tongue tip does not leave the ridge between the consonant and the final /n/ or /l/.
nodes.note: In unstressed final syllables, /n/ and /l/ can form a syllable on their own: button [ˈbʌʔn̩], little [ˈlɪɾɫ̩]. Before syllabic /n/, many Americans use a glottal stop instead of /t/.
nodes.contrast: In button and kitten, the final syllable is just /n/, with no vowel before it. Butter and kitty end with a vowel.

sentences.text: The kitten sat in the garden.
Press the little button.
The cotton was certainly expensive.
Put the bottle in the middle.
A sudden noise woke the people.
The mountain looked gentle.

nodes.name: Reduced vowels and weak forms
nodes.tongue: In unstressed function words, relax the tongue into the central schwa position.
nodes.airflow: Quick and light.
nodes.feel: Function words become short and quiet, while content words stay strong and clear.
nodes.note: Grammar words such as a, the, to, for, of, and, and can usually appear in weak forms with schwa: to /tə/, for /fɚ/, can /kən/. Using strong forms everywhere makes speech sound robotic and can change meaning: in I can go, can is weak, but in I can't go, can't keeps its full vowel.
nodes.contrast: Weak can has a schwa and almost no stress: /kən/. Can't keeps a full /æ/ vowel and is stressed, even when its final t is barely heard.

sentences.text: I want to go for a walk.
sentences.ipa: /aɪ wɑnt tə ɡoʊ fɚ ə wɔk/

sentences.text: A cup of tea and a piece of cake.
I can meet them at the station.
She was waiting for the bus.
Bread and butter is on the table.
We came from a town near the coast.
sentences.ipa: /wi keɪm frəm‿ə taʊn nɪr ðə koʊst/

nodes.name: Linking
nodes.tongue: Move directly from the last sound of one word into the first sound of the next, without stopping.
nodes.lips: Prepare the next word while finishing the current one.
nodes.airflow: Unbroken from one word to the next.
nodes.feel: Phrases feel like one long word: turn it off sounds like tur-ni-toff.
nodes.note: Americans link a final consonant to a following vowel, add a light /j/ or /w/ between vowels (the end, go on), and pronounce a linking r in far away. Recognizing linking is essential for understanding fast speech.
nodes.contrast: The small word it links to the words around it: pick it up sounds like pi-ki-tup. Listen for the extra syllable.

sentences.text: Turn it off and go on.
Pick it up and put it away.
Check it out at the end of August.
Hold on and come in.
Not at all, take an apple.
Fill it in and hand it over.
